actions.justification: MANDATORY: Identify risk factors for AKI including heart failure, diabetes, prior CKD, nephrotoxin exposure. This is time-critical and must be completed within 60 minutes.
MANDATORY: Patient has oliguria as a chief complaint. Monitoring urine output is essential to quantify severity of AKI and guide fluid management, especially with underlying heart failure.
MANDATORY: Serum creatinine is required to confirm and stage AKI severity per KDIGO criteria, and to guide management decisions.

Patient has tachycardia (HR 105), hypertension (BP 145/88), tachypnea (RR 24), and hypoxia (SpO2 91%) — formal vital signs assessment is the immediate first step to characterize severity and guide management.
BMP will provide electrolytes (potassium critical in AKI), BUN, glucose, and bicarbonate to assess metabolic derangements and severity of renal failure in this patient with confusion and oliguria.

Volume assessment is essential to differentiate pre-renal AKI from intrinsic/oliguric AKI, especially given comorbid heart failure — this will guide whether fluid resuscitation or restriction is appropriate.
Urinalysis with microscopy is essential to identify the cause of AKI (ATN casts, proteinuria, hematuria suggesting intrinsic renal disease) and has not yet been ordered.
Patient has SpO2 91%, RR 24, and confusion — arterial blood gas is critical to assess for metabolic acidosis (consistent with severe AKI), respiratory compensation, and degree of hypoxemia.

Patient has heart failure and diabetes type 2 and is likely on ACE inhibitors, metformin, diuretics, or NSAIDs — all potentially nephrotoxic or harmful in acute AKI. Immediate review and discontinuation of offending agents is a key AKI management step.
Patient has heart failure and AKI with oliguria — formal hydration/volume status assessment is critical to guide fluid management and avoid fluid overload in this complex patient.

Severe AKI (creatinine 5.8) requires urgent review of all current medications for nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, aminoglycosides) and dose adjustment for renally cleared drugs per universal safety guideline.
Urinalysis with microscopy is essential to differentiate pre-renal, intrinsic (ATN, AIN, glomerular) vs post-renal AKI and has not yet been ordered from this scenario's available action list.

FENa is essential to distinguish pre-renal AKI from intrinsic renal causes (ATN) in this oliguric patient with severe AKI (Cr 5.8). This guides fluid management decisions especially important given underlying heart failure.
Patient has confusion, tachycardia (HR 105), and SpO2 91% — lactate is needed to assess for tissue hypoperfusion/lactic acidosis as a complication of severe AKI and potential contributing factor.

Checking baseline eGFR is critical to determine if this is acute-on-chronic kidney disease vs new acute AKI, which directly impacts management decisions and prognosis in this diabetic patient with heart failure.
Creatinine 5.8 indicates severe AKI with high risk of hyperkalemia, which can cause fatal arrhythmias. Potassium monitoring is critical and urgent given oliguria and severe renal impairment.
Renal ultrasound is essential to rule out post-renal obstruction (e.g., hydronephrosis) as a reversible cause of AKI. This is a key step in identifying the etiology per AKI management guidelines.

Urine electrolytes (Na, Cr) help calculate FENa and differentiate pre-renal from intrinsic renal causes of AKI, guiding appropriate fluid management especially in this patient with heart failure comorbidity.

Patient has SpO2 of 91%, RR 24, and known heart failure. Chest X-ray is urgently needed to evaluate for pulmonary edema/fluid overload, which would contraindicate fluid resuscitation and may explain respiratory compromise.
Review AKI risk factors to identify precipitating cause (pre-renal, intrinsic, post-renal) and guide targeted management. Patient has diabetes and heart failure which are major risk factors.
CBC to evaluate for infection (elevated WBC), anemia (contributing to reduced O2 delivery and AKI), and thrombocytopenia (TTP/HUS as a cause of AKI). Not yet completed per available records.

Patient has severe AKI (Cr 5.8) with heart failure and diabetes. Nephrotoxic agents must be discontinued immediately to prevent further renal injury. This is a critical management step per KDIGO AKI guidelines.

Renal ultrasound is indicated to rule out post-renal obstruction as a cause of severe AKI. This is a standard workup step and the prior 'order_renal_ultrasound' may differ from this specific action_id.
Contrast-induced nephropathy is a common iatrogenic cause of AKI. Given the severity of renal impairment, reviewing recent contrast exposure is important to identify etiology and guide management.

Patient has severe AKI with heart failure comorbidity, SpO2 91%, and oliguria. Optimizing fluid status is critical - avoiding both under-resuscitation and fluid overload in this complex patient. This is a key management step per KDIGO AKI guidelines.

With creatinine of 5.8 and severe AKI, all nephrotoxic agents must be formally discontinued. This action ensures NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and other nephrotoxins are stopped to prevent further kidney injury.

Severe AKI (creatinine 5.8) with confusion warrants coagulation studies to evaluate for uremic coagulopathy and assess bleeding risk, which is important before any interventional procedures and for overall management.

Severe AKI with creatinine 5.8, confusion, oliguria, and SpO2 91% in a patient with heart failure warrants urgent nephrology consultation for consideration of renal replacement therapy (dialysis) and expert management guidance.
Cystatin C provides a more accurate assessment of GFR in severe AKI than creatinine alone, especially useful for medication dose adjustments and tracking kidney function trajectory in this patient.
Serial creatinine measurement is essential to monitor the trajectory of AKI (worsening vs. stabilizing) in this critically ill patient with creatinine already at 5.8 mg/dL.

Patient has severe AKI (creatinine 5.8) with heart failure comorbidity, confusion, oliguria, and SpO2 91% — nephrology/cardiology consultation is critical for coordinated management including possible RRT consideration and volume optimization in the setting of heart failure.
Urine culture is indicated to rule out infectious etiology contributing to AKI, especially given fever potential and confusion. Urinalysis already completed but culture not yet sent.

Patient may have a pre-renal component contributing to AKI. Careful, monitored crystalloid administration is appropriate given oliguria, but must be cautious given heart failure and fluid overload risk — small bolus with close monitoring of urine output and respiratory status (SpO2 91%).

Patient has severe AKI (creatinine 5.8) with tachycardia (HR 105) and SpO2 91%. While volume status has been assessed and optimize_fluid_status is already done, continued careful IV hydration support is indicated given hemodynamic stress — noting heart failure comorbidity requires cautious fluid administration to avoid worsening congestion.

Patient has severe renal impairment (creatinine 5.8, likely very low eGFR) with heart failure and diabetes. Calculating contrast volume limit is a critical safety step to prevent further AKI from any future contrast exposure, per KDIGO contrast-AKI guidelines.

Patient has severe AKI (creatinine 5.8) with known risk factors. If contrast imaging is clinically necessary, use of low osmolar contrast agent minimizes further nephrotoxic injury per KDIGO contrast-AKI guidelines. This is the only remaining available action and represents appropriate renal protection in this high-risk patient.
